For example, a user can select a percentage of a specific segment to adopt this measure while using the results from the baseline simulation for the remaining models. Units in multi-family buildings are included in the measure. Although multi- family households may not own the charging infrastructure or see its impact on their utility bills in practice, we model them consistently with other housing types, treating EV energy as a direct household energy cost. We also assume that multi-family chargers are always available, which may not be true in practice, and therefore the charging event durations may not reflect actual events. 4 This report is available at no cost from the National Laboratory of the Rockies (NLR) at www.nlr.gov/publications. 4 Modeling Approach 4.1 Methodology To model baseline residential EV charging demand in ResStock, our approach: (1) characterizes regional inputs that affect EV battery parameters, driving behavior, and charger characteristics; (2) assigns these inputs as arguments to individual dwelling unit models; (3) generates occupancy-driven charging and discharging schedules; and (4) simulates building energy models with integrated EVs. We associate each EV with an at-home charger, and report only the charging energy of the dwelling unit, as charging energy away from home is not modeled. No vehicle-to-building energy exchange is considered in ResStock. To apply this measure to the baseline, we repeat Steps 2–4 using updated inputs to assign EV ownership and charger. More detailed information regarding baseline EV modeling and scheduling in ResStock can be found in Speake et al. (2025), which describes the EV stock characterization, model input generation, battery modeling, and analysis of baseline results. Electric Vehicle Stock Characterization Included in the baseline ResStock inputs are probability distributions that describe the likelihood of EV-related attributes being assigned to dwelling units. These EV-related inputs are part of ResStock’s broader stock characterization process, which defines detailed building, occupant, and technology characteristics for the U.S. residential building stock (see Section 3 Reyna et al. [2025] for more detail). EV input distributions are sampled to produce EV ownership profiles for each building model. The baseline of ResStock assigns each dwelling unit a value for EV ownership, the at-home charging fraction, the vehicle type that provides the battery capacity and efficiency, and the VMT per year. If a dwelling unit has an EV, an EV charger is applied, and its power draw is determined based on the charger level. Plug-in hybrid electric vehicles are not currently modeled in ResStock. The ResStock EV implementation draws data from the TEMPO™ model (Muratori et al. 2021), EIA RECS 2020 (U.S. EIA 2020), the National Household Travel Survey (Federal Highway Administration 2022), vehicle registration data from Experian1, the No Place Like Home study (Ge et al. 2021), and the Autonomie model2. The distributions of these options reflect 2023 saturation levels of EV technology and operation in the United States, ensuring that EV-related measures capture expected diversity3.
